I have farmed these 9 mu for 30 years. My mother taught me, and now I know the land better than I know my own hands. We grow wheat and maize, one after the other, because that is what this soil wants. My sons work in the city and send money home, so I can buy good inputs, but I do not waste money on things that do not help.

For wheat, I will sow in October after turning the soil with the rotary tiller. I use improved seed — about 30 jin per mu. I put down compound fertilizer as basal, the 18-22-5 blend that the shop sells, about 100 jin per mu. At green-up or jointing, I topdress with urea. I irrigate three times from the well: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing, and once at heading or grain filling. I spray for weeds once, and for insects and diseases two or three times depending on what I see in the field. If the weather is kind, I expect about 1000 jin per mu.

After harvesting wheat in early June, I plant maize immediately without plowing — no-tillage, because there is no time between crops and the wheat straw helps keep moisture in the ground. I buy hybrid seed, Nongda or something similar, about one package per mu. I apply compound fertilizer, the 28-6-6 type, about 80 jin per mu at sowing, and sometimes I add urea at the big trumpet stage if the plants look yellow. Maize needs less water than wheat here; I irrigate twice, usually when the leaves start to curl and again during grain filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice. A normal year gives me about 1100 jin per mu.

I do not use much extra potassium because the compound fertilizer already has some, and our soil here has enough from years of straw return. I also do not change what works. My neighbors and I all do more or less the same thing — if someone gets a new idea, we watch them for a year first.
